summary: Defines two PIM Join/Prune attributes for building multicast trees between LISP sites. They let a receiver site choose unicast or multicast underlay transport and convey the receiver ETR's RLOC address. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: When a show is sent to viewers in different buildings, each building tells the sender how to deliver it and where to send it.

subtitle: Two PIM Join/Prune attributes that let LISP receiver sites pick unicast or multicast transport and report their RLOC.

tldr.problem: When a multicast root and its receivers sit in different LISP sites, the Join/Prune message says nothing about whether the receiver wants multicast or unicast head-end replication, and its outer source address may not be the RLOC the receiver wants to use.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the Transport attribute (type 5) to choose multicast (0) or unicast (1), and the Receiver RLOC attribute (type 6) to carry the receiver ETR's RLOC address to the root ITR's control plane.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental specification. It is updated by RFC 9798.

today: RFC 8059 is an Experimental specification, and the unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 9798. The RFC text itself describes the work as published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation.

sections.title: The Problem Between LISP Sites
sections.content:
In the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), multicast trees that span sites need a unicast LISP-encapsulated Join/Prune message sent from an ETR on the receiver site to an ITR on the root site. That message names the (root-EID,G) state to create but conveys nothing about whether the receiver can or wants to use multicast as the underlying transport.

The authors note that wide deployment of multicast connectivity between LISP sites is unlikely to happen soon, and some implementations focus first on unicast transport with head-end replication. The document therefore lets the receiver say which it wants.

A second gap is the receiver's RLOC. Providers may apply uRPF policies that require the outer source address to be the address of the core-facing interface, which may not be the RLOC on which the site wants to receive a flow.
sections.eli5: The sender does not know if the receiving building can get a broadcast or needs a personal delivery, or which door to use. These attributes let the building say so.

sections.title: Using PIM Join/Prune Attributes
sections.content:
The attributes follow the format defined in RFC 5384, which lets Join/Prune messages carry Type-Length-Value (TLV) attributes attached to individual sources. Because these attributes are typically the same for all sources in a message, the document RECOMMENDS the hierarchical scheme of RFC 7887, which lets one attribute in the Upstream Neighbor Address field apply to all sources.

LISP Tunnel Routers do not exchange PIM Hello messages, so there is no Hello option to negotiate support. Systems that support unicast head-end replication are assumed to support these attributes.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a note for every single item, you can put one sticky note on the whole package.

sections.title: The Transport Attribute
sections.content:
The Transport attribute lets a receiver pick the underlying transport. Root sites with multicast connectivity can use multicast replication, but not every receiver site has it, so a root should be ready to support a mixture of multicast and unicast output state.

The attribute has type 5 and length 1, and always has the F (transitive) bit set to zero. Its one-octet value is 0 for multicast and 1 for unicast; values 2 to 255 may be assigned in the future.

An encoded address MUST NOT carry more than one Transport attribute. If it does, or if the value is unknown, the root ITR MUST discard all affected Join/Prune sources.
sections.eli5: It is a checkbox on the request: deliver by broadcast, or deliver to me personally. Fill in two boxes or an unknown one, and the request is thrown away.

sections.title: The Receiver ETR RLOC Attribute
sections.content:
For unicast head-end replication, the root ITR's PIM control plane keeps an outgoing interface list entry for each receiver ETR and its RLOC, so it can unicast-encapsulate multicast data to each one. The RLOC could be guessed from the outer source address of the Join/Prune message, but uRPF checks and load-balancing policy can make that the wrong address.

The Receiver RLOC attribute (type 6) carries the right address: an Address Family octet defined in RFC 7761 followed by the RLOC. Its length is the address length plus one octet for the family. The root ITR MUST discard affected sources if the attribute is duplicated, the address family is unknown, or the address length is wrong.

Receiver ETRs must also be tracked for root-EID mobility. When the root moves to a new site, the old root ITR learns of it through a Map-Notify and sends a Solicit-Map-Request to each receiver ETR. The receiver then looks up the new root ITR, sends a PIM prune to the old one and a join to the new one.
sections.eli5: The receiver writes its exact address on the request so deliveries go to the right door. If the sender moves, the old sender tells everyone to look up the new address.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Security of Join/Prune attributes is only as good as the security of the PIM packet. These attributes neither enhance nor diminish privacy or authenticity. A site that can deliver a Join/Prune message can also append these attributes, as the general considerations in RFC 5384 say.

IANA assigned attribute types 5 (Transport) and 6 (Receiver RLOC) and created the "PIM Join/Prune Transport Types" registry with IETF Review as the policy and values in the range 0 to 255. Values 0 (multicast) and 1 (unicast) are assigned here.
sections.eli5: The new notes are only as trustworthy as the envelope they come in, and the registry is a public list of what each number means.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: End-of-Attributes bit; 1 if this is the last attribute.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value; MUST be 1.
